It shares the sampler branch with `voronoicells` and `voronoipillows` and adds gradient fields; the known defect is the same as for voronoicells: blurry smudges at sharp junctions.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the gradient strength of 0.35, the tones (plate 0.7, tone floor 0.3), the base roughness of 0.3, the seam roughness increment of 0.4, the relief of 0.0012, the emerald tones and the 0.4 m nominal tile are authored choices (I looked at only one preview). To share the branch I added the field `facet: 0` to the `voronoicells` and `voronoipillows` presets; the gradient term adds 0 when facet is 0 (the values do not change) and the `smoothstep(clamp())` of the tone is applied only when facet is non-zero, so their behaviour is unchanged and both of their tests (8 test cases each) still pass; I did not compare the outputs before and after the change bit for bit and rely only on those tests. The known defects are the same as for voronoicells (blurry smudges, no independently rewritten site model, and tests that only check observable behaviour). Error record: the first version of my test asserted that the colour spread of every plate is above 0.2, and all four seeds failed (the smallest plate spread was only 0.083); I had measured only the largest spread over all plates (0.31–0.36) and not the distribution; after measuring the distribution (smallest 0.029–0.036, median 0.135–0.175, mean 0.141–0.168) I changed the assertion to a mean spread between 0.13 and 0.18, a largest spread above 0.28 and every plate below 0.4, and it passed; the mistake was in my test expectation, not in the sampler.

It reuses the voronoicells sampler (which now serves `voronoicells`, `voronoipillows` and `voronoifacets`): at start-up every cell additionally gets a gradient `gradientX = 0.35·2·(hash − 0.5)` and `gradientY` from the internal hash (with two different seed salts); at sampling time, over the 25 sites of the 5×5 neighbouring cells, besides the weights `w_i = exp(−(d_i − d_min)/0.02)` the code keeps the displacement `(fromX, fromY)` from the sample to each site, and the tone is `Σ w_i·(tone_i + gradientX_i·fromX_i + gradientY_i·fromY_i) / Σ w_i`, limited to [0, 1] by `smoothstep(clamp(tone))`; the boundary measure (Gini impurity), color, height and so on are as in voronoicells: color is `0.05 + 0.7·(0.3 + 0.7·tone)·(1 − edge) + 0.02·edge + 0.02·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`, height is `0.8·(1 − edge)·(0.8 + 0.2·tone) + 0.06·grain`, `roughness = 0.3 + 0.4·edge`, `occlusion = 1 − 0.45·edge` and metallic is 0; the cache totals five `Float64Array(64)`, four `Float64Array(25)`, one `Int32Array(25)` and a `Float64Array(128²)`, 134,432 B plus 100 B, all lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Defaults are a 0.4 m nominal tile and 0.0012 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Each sample needs about 25 distance and exponential evaluations; I did not measure this material's time. Measured (tool-run): at 512² for the four seeds (0/1/0xffffffff/7), splitting the pixels with occlusion above 0.97 into 4-connected regions (wrapped) gives exactly 64 regions for every seed; the region sizes are 1,325–1,739 pixels at the smallest and 4,681–5,242 at the largest; the colour spread inside a plate (maximum minus minimum) has a mean of 0.141–0.168, a median of 0.135–0.175, a minimum of 0.029–0.036 and a maximum of 0.307–0.356 (for the flat plates of voronoicells the maximum is only 0.0654, from the grain); the mean colours of the regions run from 0.2595–0.2609 (darkest) to 0.7445–0.7469 (brightest); these interior pixels cover 74.54%–75.93%; at 256² (seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7) color is 0.0619–0.0626 to 0.7589–0.7592 with a mean of 0.4211–0.4377 (it varies with the seed), roughness is 0.3 to about 0.6997, the lowest AO is 0.5503–0.5504 and height is at most 0.8569–0.8583 relief; at 512² (four seeds) color is 0.0610–0.0617 to 0.7595–0.7597 with a mean of 0.4211–0.4377 and height is at most 0.8588–0.8592 relief; the interior masks (512²) of seeds 0 and 1 differ on 36.3% of pixels; a second-difference C1 scan (seed 0, including the cell grid lines and 16,384 golden-ratio points) finds no point above 0.03; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (67.9, 125.1, 105.3), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0468 and the minimum z component is 252. I viewed the preview (seed 7): emerald-green polygonal plates, each with a light-to-dark gradient from one side to the other, separated by dark thin seams, with blurry smudges only at a few sharp junctions. No new API or dependency; Worker, cache and texture ownership follow the existing paths; this paragraph does not claim browser gallery verification.

`multiplicativeorder` adds a multiplicative order table, bringing the current catalog from 1010 to 1011 kinds (1012 gallery choices including plain). It is a 48×48 grid of squares in which cell (col, row) stands for the residue `a = col + 1` (1 to 48) modulo `n = row + 2` (2 to 49): if a and n share a factor, a has no multiplicative order and the cell is painted in the darkest tone (887 cells); otherwise it is toned by the multiplicative order `ord_n(a)` (the least positive k with `a^k ≡ 1 (mod n)`) divided by `φ(n)` (the number of residues coprime to n), raised to the power 1.5: a ratio of 1 means a is a primitive root modulo n (406 cells; these exist only for n equal to 2, 4, a prime power or twice a prime power, which is a standard fact of number theory that I did not verify in the tests), 189 cells have order 1 (a ≡ 1), and the largest order is 46 (a primitive root modulo the prime 47). It shows ice-blue on deep navy, the bright cells looking like irregularly scattered dots and short lines. The cells are rounded raised squares showing gaps through height and AO, and the seed shifts the whole table around the torus. It shares the cell shape with number-theory tables such as `totienttable` and `divisorcount` (and reuses the Mandelbrot tiles' 'inside' tone treatment for the cells without an order). It only shows the order ratios of the first 48×48 residues; it does not prove or illustrate any theorem of number theory.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the toneExponent of 1.5, the toneFloor of 0.14, the toneSpan of 0.7, the insideTone of 0.02, the ice-blue and deep navy tones and the 0.3 m nominal tile are authored choices (I looked at only one preview). I did not check whether the residues a mod n for a ≥ n create visible periodic repeats in the table (for example the rows for small moduli such as n = 2 and 3 are periodic); that is a property of this way of assigning values. The cell shape and tone combination reuse the totienttable parameters. The tests passed on the first run with no need to adjust ranges; the number of cells without an order (887), of primitive-root cells (406), of cells of order 1 (189) and the largest order 46 are values computed in the test with independent repeated multiplication and coprime counting, and were not compared with theoretical values.

At start-up the code checks `gcd(a, n)` for every cell (`n = row + 2`, `a = col + 1`): if it is not 1 the cell is recorded as `−1` (no multiplicative order); otherwise the order is found by repeated multiplication (starting from `power = a % n`, multiplying by `a % n` modulo n until it returns to 1, the count being the order), `φ(n)` is counted by coprime residues, and the tone is `(order / φ(n))^1.5`; at sampling time every cell uses one compact-support rounded-square kernel (a quartic superellipse through smoothstep, exactly zero before the cell boundary, so the cell lookup never jumps and the field is C1): for `tone ≥ 0` color is `0.04 + (0.14 + 0.7·tone − 0.04)·mask + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`, and for `tone < 0` `0.02` replaces `0.14 + 0.7·tone`; height is `0.8·dome·(0.88 + 0.12·tone)` (0.5 replaces the bracket for cells without an order) `+ 0.08·grain`, `occlusion = 1 − 0.4·(1 − mask)`, roughness is fixed at 0.4 and metallic is 0; the cache totals a `Float64Array(2304)` of 18,432 B plus a `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B, 149,504 B in all, all lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Defaults are a 0.3 m nominal tile and 0.0008 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Each sample does a constant number of operations; I did not measure the time. Measured (tool-run): of the 2304 cells 887 have no multiplicative order, 406 are primitive roots, 189 have order 1 and the largest order is 46; on a 256² grid (seeds 0/1/0xffffffff) the lit area (color>0.5) covers 12.50%–12.64%, color is 0.0055–0.0058 to 0.8541–0.8544 with a mean of 0.2146–0.2153, the lowest AO is 0.6 and height is at most 0.8753–0.8768 relief; on a 512² grid (seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7) the lit area covers 12.47%–12.74%, color is 0.0052–0.0054 to 0.8545–0.8547 with a mean of 0.2142–0.2163 and height is at most 0.8772–0.8784 relief; for each seed exactly one torus shift (seed 0: (28, 20), 1: (38, 22), 0xffffffff: (20, 37), 7: (37, 9)) makes the colours at the 2304 cell centres match the tones that the test rewrites independently, within a maximum error of 0.0150 (the error comes from the grain; the test's threshold is 0.03); between seeds 0 and 1, 59.9% of the cell centres differ in colour by more than 0.05, and the light masks (512²) differ on 20.4% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (45.4, 59.2, 78.2), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0300 and the minimum z component is 253. I viewed the preview (seed 7): ice-blue rounded squares scattered into an irregular pattern of dots and short lines on deep navy, with a few rows repeating regularly. No new API or dependency; Worker, cache and texture ownership follow the existing paths; this paragraph does not claim browser gallery verification.

`sandpileidentity` adds a sandpile identity, bringing the current catalog from 1009 to 1010 kinds (1011 gallery choices including plain). It draws the identity element of the abelian sandpile group of a 64×64 grid: every cell holds a pile of sand, a cell with 4 grains topples and gives one grain to each of its four neighbours, and grains that fall off the border are lost into a sink; the identity is obtained by Dhar's method: stabilise twice the maximal stable configuration of 3 grains per cell (6 grains per cell), subtract the result from 6 to get the remainder, and stabilise once more. The result is a pattern of heights (0 to 3 grains): 396 cells are 0, 152 are 1, 1,476 are 2 and 2,072 are 3, symmetric left-right, top-bottom and across the diagonal (transpose), forming an ornate mandala-like design; the four height levels map to shades of gold (0 darkest, 3 brightest), and the edges and the large flat square areas are characteristic of the identity. The seed only shifts the whole 64×64 pattern around the torus; because the identity itself is not periodic (its border is a sink), a framed seam formed by the pattern's border is visible when tiled. It is only a visualisation of this mathematical object, not a real sandpile.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the size of 64×64, the tanh sharpness of 8, the tone (span 0.72), the gold and dark brown colours and the 0.5 m nominal tile are authored choices (I looked at only one preview). I did not check the original literature for Dhar's identity formula; it is written from my understanding (stabilise twice the maximal configuration, subtract, stabilise again), and the tests check it through the necessary property of an identity, that `e + e` stabilises back to `e`, and through an independently written sweeping toppling algorithm (different from the stack-based one in the sampler), rather than relying on the formula alone; **this only shows that the result is an element of the group with `e + e = e`, and I did not separately verify that it is the identity for all recurrent configurations**. The tiling seam is a consequence of the design and I did not try to hide it. The relief reuses 0.0008 without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0297). One test failed along the way: I copied the roughness check from the T-square test (expecting the roughness to drop to about 0.2 on lines), but this material has a constant roughness of 0.4, so the failing part was the copied expectation, not the sampler; after I changed it to check that the roughness equals the preset value the test passed.

At start-up (computed once per process and cached by size, shared by all seeds and samplers) the all-6 configuration on the `64 × 64` grid is stabilised (a stack processes every cell with height ≥ 4: `toppled = floor(height/4)`, the cell loses `4·toppled` and each of its existing neighbours gains `toppled`, grains beyond the border vanish), the result is subtracted from 6 and stabilised once more, giving the identity as a `Uint8Array(4096)` (in my timing script the first stabilisation took 2,323,784 topplings and the second 881,488, and the whole computation took about 69 ms in bun, a single measurement, not a benchmark); every sampler builds one `Float64Array(4096)` per height threshold 1, 2 and 3 (1 where the height is at least the threshold, shifted by the seed's torus shift), and at sampling time each is blended by `latticeField` (C1 smoothstep) and re-sharpened with `0.5 + 0.5·tanh(8·(field − 0.5))`, the three summed and divided by 3 giving the tone: color is `0.05 + 0.72·tone + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`, height is `0.8·tone + 0.2·grain`, roughness is fixed at 0.4, AO is always 1 and metallic is 0; the cache per sampler is 3×4,096 + 128² = 28,672 Float64 values / 229,376 B, plus the shared 4,096 B identity, all lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile and 0.0008 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Each sample does a constant number of operations; I did not measure the sampling time. Measured (tool-run): the identity that the test computes with an independent sweeping algorithm has 396/152/1,476/2,072 cells of height 0/1/2/3, is symmetric left-right, top-bottom and under transpose, and `e + e` stabilises back to `e`; at seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7: on a 256² grid the lit area (color>0.5) covers 86.28%–86.31% (seeds 0/1/0xffffffff), color is 0.0364–0.0374 to 0.7840–0.7844 with a mean of 0.6030–0.6031, roughness is always 0.4, AO is always 1 and height is at most 0.9950–0.9973 relief; on a 512² grid the lit area covers 85.87%–85.88%, color is 0.0356–0.0358 to 0.7846–0.7847 with a mean of 0.6034–0.6036 and height is at most 0.9984–0.9991 relief; each seed's 64×64 nodes (sampled at the nodes) match the independent model at exactly one torus shift (seed 0: (52, 10), 1: (14, 48), 0xffffffff: (9, 46), 7: (6, 37)) over all 4,096 nodes within a maximum error of 0.0150 (equal to the grain's maximum amplitude 0.03×0.5; the test's threshold is 0.03), with 3,548 lit nodes (heights 2 or 3, = 1,476 + 2,072) each time; seeds 0 and 1 differ in 23.3% of the lit nodes; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (165.0, 143.7, 93.7), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0297 and the minimum z component is 253. I viewed the preview (seed 7): dark dotted ornaments and mandala-like designs on a golden ground, with large flat square areas. No new API or dependency; Worker, cache and texture ownership follow the existing paths; this paragraph does not claim browser gallery verification.

`voronoipillows` adds Voronoi pillows, bringing the current catalog from 1008 to 1009 kinds (1010 gallery choices including plain). The same Voronoi plates as `voronoicells` (one jittered site per cell of an 8×8 grid, soft-weight partition, 64 plates and dark thin seams), but the height of every plate is a raised dome (pillow-shaped): the height falls smoothly with the distance to the weighted mean site, highest at the middle of the plate and sinking to the bottom near the seams; the colour is terracotta (each plate with its own random lightness) and the seams are still dark, rough and AO-darkened. The seed decides the sites and tones. It is a schematic clay-tile or pillow look, not real clay, and nothing real was compared. It shares the sampler branch with `voronoicells` and only the preset differs, plus new dome fields. The known defect is the same as for voronoicells: blurry smudges at sharp junctions.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the dome radius of 0.55 cells, the dome height of 0.5, the plate base height of 0.4, the roughness of 0.45, the relief of 0.0016, the terracotta tones and the 0.4 m nominal tile are authored choices (I looked at only one preview, and it shows only the base colour and not the domes, so the domes are verified through the probe and the height statistics of the tests, and **I never saw the lit 3D appearance**). To share the branch I added the fields `domeRadius: 0.55` and `domeHeight: 0` to the `voronoicells` preset (a dome height of 0 leaves its behaviour and values unchanged, and its 8 test cases still pass). The known defects are the same as for voronoicells (blurry smudges, no independently rewritten site model, and tests that only check observable behaviour). The tests passed on the first run with no need to adjust ranges.

It reuses the voronoicells sampler (which now serves `voronoicells` and `voronoipillows`): after the weights `w_i = exp(−(d_i − d_min)/0.02)` over the 25 sites of the 5×5 neighbouring cells, besides the weighted mean tone and the Gini impurity (the boundary measure) it computes the weighted mean distance `Σw_i·d_i / Σw_i` (smooth, because it is a smooth function of the normalised weights) and the dome term is `domeHeight·(1 − edge)·smoothstep(clamp(1 − mean distance/0.55))`; height is `0.4·(1 − edge)·(0.8 + 0.2·tone) + 0.5·(1 − edge)·dome + 0.08·grain` (at most about 0.98, never above 1); the rest is as in voronoicells: color is `0.06 + 0.62·(0.35 + 0.65·tone)·(1 − edge) + 0.02·edge + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`, `roughness = 0.45 + 0.3·edge`, `occlusion = 1 − 0.45·edge`, metallic is 0, and the cache is that of voronoicells (133,008 B plus 100 B). Defaults are a 0.4 m nominal tile and 0.0016 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Each sample needs about 25 distance and exponential evaluations; I did not measure this material's time. Measured (tool-run): at 512² for the four seeds (0/1/0xffffffff/7), splitting the pixels with occlusion above 0.97 into 4-connected regions (wrapped) gives exactly 64 regions for every seed; the region sizes are 1,326–1,850 pixels at the smallest and 4,559–4,956 at the largest; the colour spread inside any region is at most 0.0687; the mean colours of the regions run from 0.2770–0.2825 (darkest) to 0.6731–0.6768 (brightest); these interior pixels cover 74.27%–75.37%; the height difference inside each plate (maximum minus minimum, in relief units) is 0.5297–0.5966 (about half the relief; a flat plate would vary only by the grain) and the peak height of each plate is 0.8482–0.9677 relief; at 256² (seeds 0/1/0xffffffff) color is 0.0674–0.0689 to 0.6880–0.6915 with a mean of 0.4115–0.4312, roughness is 0.45 to 0.7497–0.7498, the lowest AO is 0.5503–0.5504 and height is at most 0.9585–0.9625 relief; at 512² (four seeds) color is 0.0667–0.0676 to 0.6894–0.6941 with a mean of 0.4115–0.4312 and height is at most 0.9646–0.9677 relief; the interior masks (512²) of seeds 0 and 1 differ on 35.8% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (116.4, 78.6, 59.4), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0820 and the minimum z component is 250. `voronoicells` adds Voronoi cells, bringing the current catalog from 1007 to 1008 kinds (1009 gallery choices including plain). It is the engine's first material of the Voronoi (nearest-site) family: on a periodic 8×8 grid every cell holds one jittered site (at most ±0.4 cell widths from the cell centre), 64 sites in all, each with a random tone; the whole texture is split by the nearest site into 64 polygonal plates, each plate with one tone (blue-grey, from dark to light), with thin dark seams between plates (rougher, darkened by AO and lower in height). The borders use soft weights (see the technical details) rather than a hard nearest-site lookup, so the field is smooth (C1) and the seam width is a fixed small amount. The seed only decides the sites and tones (every seed gives a different arrangement of plates). It is a schematic slab or mosaic look, not real stone, and the lightness of the plates is random and not compared with any real rock. A known defect: where the edges meet at very sharp angles the seam turns into a small blurry triangular smudge (a few are visible in the preview).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the 8×8 cells, the jitter of 0.8, the softness of 0.02, the edgeGain of 10, the tones (plate 0.62, tone floor 0.35, seam 0.02), the blue-grey colours, the relief of 0.0012 and the 0.4 m nominal tile are authored choices. Adjustments and error record: (1) the first version used a softness of 0.04 and an edgeGain of 6, and the preview showed several blurry smudges; changing to a softness of 0.02 and an edgeGain of 10 made the smudges smaller but did not remove them (I looked at three previews, the last two of which are byte-identical after I tidied the code). (2) The first version used a 3×3 window of neighbouring cells and the C1 test failed (second-difference ratio 332.8): scanning point by point with a probe (seed 0) found 213 (point, axis, channel) combinations above 0.03; the cause is that the window changes side when the point crosses a cell boundary, and the site that drops out is sometimes within only about a tenth of a cell width of the nearest distance, so its weight cannot be ignored and creates a slope jump; with a 5×5 window the same scan finds none above the threshold and the statistics are identical to the earlier ones (to 1e-15). The tests passed after changing to 5×5. (3) I did not rewrite the site model independently for this material: the sites come from an internal hash, and the tests check only observable behaviour (64 plates, one tone per plate, the properties of the seams, C1 and periodicity), **without comparing site coordinates**.

At start-up, on the periodic 8×8 grid, the site x and y offsets (`0.8·(hash − 0.5)` cell widths) and the tone (`hash`) of every cell are computed from the internal hash (three different seed salts); at sampling time the code computes, for the 5×5 cells around the sample's cell (25 sites in all, positions in unwrapped coordinates and cell indices taken modulo), the distances `d_i` and the nearest distance `d_min`, with weights `w_i = exp(−(d_i − d_min) / 0.02)` (shifting by the nearest distance only avoids numerical underflow and does not change the result after normalisation); the tone is the weighted mean, the boundary measure is the Gini impurity `1 − Σ(w_i / Σw)²` (0 inside a plate, 1/2 where two plates meet) and `edge = 1 − exp(−10·impurity)`: color is `0.06 + 0.62·(0.35 + 0.65·tone)·(1 − edge) + 0.02·edge + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`, height is `0.8·(1 − edge)·(0.8 + 0.2·tone) + 0.08·grain`, `roughness = 0.4 + 0.3·edge`, `occlusion = 1 − 0.45·edge` and metallic is 0; the cache totals three `Float64Array(64)`, two `Float64Array(25)`, one `Int32Array(25)` and a `Float64Array(128²)`, 133,008 B plus 100 B, all lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Defaults are a 0.4 m nominal tile and 0.0012 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Each sample needs about 25 distance and exponential evaluations; I measured a 512² maps generation only three times (seeds 0, 1 and 2, once each) at about 143–182 ms, which are single measurements, not a benchmark, and I did not compare them with other materials. Measured (tool-run): at 512² for the four seeds (0/1/0xffffffff/7), splitting the pixels with occlusion above 0.97 (far from the seams) into 4-connected regions (wrapped) gives exactly 64 regions for every seed; the region sizes are 974–1,851 pixels at the smallest and 4,536–5,019 at the largest; the colour spread inside any region is at most 0.0654; the mean colours of the regions run from 0.2764–0.2892 (darkest) to 0.6676–0.6765 (brightest); these interior pixels cover 74.47%–75.25%; at 256² (seeds 0/1/0xffffffff) color is 0.0668–0.0694 to 0.6842–0.6902 with a mean of 0.3962–0.4315 (it varies with the seed), roughness is 0.4 to about 0.6998, the lowest AO is 0.5503–0.5505 and height is at most 0.8734–0.8754 relief; at 512² (four seeds) color is 0.0664–0.0671 to 0.6850–0.6938 with a mean of 0.3959–0.4315 and height is at most 0.8755–0.8790 relief; the interior masks (512²) of seeds 0 and 1 differ on 35.9% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (87.3, 99.6, 111.6), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0468 and the minimum z component is 252. I viewed the final preview (seed 7): blue-grey polygonal plates with dark thin seams and varying plate tones, with blurry smudges only at a few sharp junctions. No new API or dependency; Worker, cache and texture ownership follow the existing paths; this paragraph does not claim browser gallery verification.

`cantordust` adds a Cantor dust, bringing the current catalog from 1006 to 1007 kinds (1008 gallery choices including plain). It draws the order-4 two-dimensional Cantor set (Cantor dust) on an 81×81 lattice: split the square into 3×3, keep only the four corners and remove the plus-shaped five blocks (the four edges and the centre), repeated four times; that is, a cell (x, y) survives when at every pair of base-3 digits from the coarsest to the finest neither the digit of x nor the digit of y is 1. There are 4⁴ = 256 surviving cells, drawn as small golden dots, and the other cells are shaded in different dark tones by the level at which they were removed: the coarsest level (the plus of five 27×27 blocks, 3,645 cells) is brightest and the finer levels (1,620, 720 and 320 cells) get darker in turn, so the whole looks like constellations of dots with at least two cells between neighbouring dots. The seed only shifts the whole lattice around the torus. It shares the sampler branch with `vicsekfractal` and only the survival rule differs (the Vicsek fractal keeps the plus, the Cantor dust keeps the four corners). It is only a schematic fractal pattern, not an exact mathematical diagram.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the order 4, the tanh sharpness of 8, the tones (line 0.72, depth 0.14), the golden and dark indigo colours and the 0.5 m nominal tile are authored choices (I looked at only one preview). Very little of the image is bright (about 3%) and most of it is the dark brownish depth tone; I did not try enlarging the dots. To share the branch I added a field `rule: 0` to the `vicsekfractal` preset (0 = plus, 2 = Cantor dust), which does not change its behaviour or values, and its tests still pass; I did not implement rule 1 (the X shape), so no preset uses it. The relief reuses 0.0008 without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0426). The tests passed on the first run with no need to adjust ranges; the numbers of cells per level and of surviving cells in the test come from a model rewritten independently by subdivision and agree with my closed-form calculation (5·27², 4·5·9², 16·5·9, 64·5).

It reuses the sampler branch of vicsekfractal (which now serves `vicsekfractal` and `cantordust`): at start-up, on an `81 × 81` lattice, the code checks every cell level by level (`unit = 3^(3 − level)`, asking whether the base-3 digits of x and y at that level are 1); rule 0 (Vicsek) records that level as the level of removal when neither digit is 1, and rule 2 (Cantor dust) when either digit is 1; surviving cells get `marks = 1`, removed cells get `marks = 0` and `depth = (4 − level) / 4`, and the cells are written into two `Float64Array`s shifted by the seed's torus shift; at sampling time it is identical to vicsekfractal: `latticeField` (C1 smoothstep) blends the survival map and `0.5 + 0.5·tanh(8·(pattern − 0.5))` re-sharpens it, a second `latticeField` blends the depth map, color is `0.05 + 0.72·line + 0.14·depth·(1 − line) + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`, height is `0.8·line + 0.2·grain`, roughness drops by 0.2 on the line (base 0.4), AO is always 1 and metallic is 0; the cache totals 81² × 2 + 128² = 29,506 Float64 values / 236,048 B of lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). `tsquarefractal` adds a T-square fractal, bringing the current catalog from 1005 to 1006 kinds (1007 gallery choices including plain). It draws the order-5 T-square fractal on a 64×64 lattice: first a square of side 32 at the centre, then squares of half the side centred on the four corners of every square, five levels in all (sides 32, 16, 8, 4 and 2; 1, 4, 16, 64 and 256 squares, 341 in all); the squares overlap, and every covered cell remembers the deepest level that covers it (the smallest squares are drawn on top). 3,124 cells are covered (76.3% of the 4,096), with 324, 432, 576, 768 and 1,024 cells at deepest levels 0 to 4, and the 972 uncovered cells form a dark brown skeleton of crosses and T shapes; the covered area is cream, and the deeper the level the brighter. The seed only shifts the whole lattice around the torus. It is only a schematic fractal pattern, not an exact mathematical diagram, and it is the covered area (not the outlines of the squares) that is bright.

`vicsekfractal` adds a Vicsek fractal, bringing the current catalog from 1004 to 1005 kinds (1006 gallery choices including plain). It draws the order-4 Vicsek fractal (the plus-shaped fractal) on an 81×81 lattice: split the square into 3×3, keep the five blocks of the plus and remove the four corners, repeated four times; that is, a cell (x, y) survives when at every pair of base-3 digits (digit of x, digit of y) from the coarsest to the finest at least one of the two equals 1. There are 5⁴ = 625 surviving cells, drawn as thin gold lines (the finest level is a plus arm one cell wide), and the other cells are shaded in different dark teal tones by the level at which they were removed: the coarsest level (the four 27×27 corners, 2,916 cells) is brightest and the finer levels (1,620, 900 and 500 cells) get darker in turn. The seed only shifts the whole lattice around the torus. It is a block fractal like `sierpinskicarpet`, but the plus shape instead of a removed centre, with the surviving cells as slightly raised thin lines (higher than their surroundings) rather than recessed squares as in `sierpinskicarpet`. It is only a schematic fractal pattern, not an exact mathematical diagram.

`squarekoch` adds a square Koch island, bringing the current catalog from 1003 to 1004 kinds (1005 gallery choices including plain). A thin salmon-pink line on a dark oxblood ground traces the order-3 type 1 quadratic Koch island: starting from `F+F+F+F` (a square) and replacing every `F` by `F+F−F−F+F` three times gives a closed loop of 500 unit steps and 376 distinct lattice points (the end returns to the start); unlike the Minkowski sausage (`minkowskisausage`, which uses `F+F−F−FF+F+F−F`), the edges of this island touch each other at corners (none of the 500 edges is walked twice, but some of the 376 vertices are visited more than once); its bounding box is 27×27 cells on a 32×32-cell torus, leaving about 4 cells of empty space between it and the island of the neighbouring tile so that they do not join; the line is a third of a cell wide with a faint glow outside it. The seed only shifts the whole curve around the torus. It is a schematic fractal trace, not a real island or map. It shares the trace sampler branch with `dragoncurve`, `peanocurve`, `levycurve` and `minkowskisausage`, and only the vertex list and replacement rule differ.

`radicaltable` adds a radical table, bringing the current catalog from 1002 to 1003 kinds (1004 gallery choices including plain). It is a 48×48 grid of squares in which cell (col, row) stands for the integer `n = row·48 + col + 1` (1 to 2304) and is toned by `ln(rad(n)) / ln(n)`, where `rad(n)` is the product of all distinct prime factors of n (the radical): squarefree numbers (1400 of them; n = 1 is defined as ratio 1) have ratio 1 and are brightest; prime powers `p^k` have ratio `1/k` (for example 4 gives 1/2, 8 gives 1/3 and 2048 gives the smallest, 1/11); the ratio is then squared to widen the differences; multiples of 4, 8 and 9 leave dark stripes and diagonals, in pale sage green on dark green. The cells are rounded raised squares showing gaps through height and AO, and the seed shifts the whole table around the torus. It shares the cell shape with number-theory tables such as `divisorcount` and `totienttable`, only the values and tones differ. It only shows the radical ratios of the first 2304 positive integers; it does not prove or illustrate the abc conjecture.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the toneExponent of 2, the toneFloor of 0.14, the toneSpan of 0.7, the sage green and dark green tones and the 0.3 m nominal tile are authored choices (I looked at only one preview). The cell shape and tone combination reuse the divisorcount parameters and were not retuned for the radical. The tests passed on the first run with no need to adjust ranges. Most cells are bright (squarefree numbers are about 61% of the table), so the whole is on the bright side; this follows from the way values are assigned and is not a defect. The relief reuses 0.0008 without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0296).

At start-up a sieve computes the radical for `n ≤ 2304` (set `rad(n) = 1`, and for every prime `q` that has not yet been multiplied into itself — that is, `rad(q) = 1` at that point — do `rad(m) *= q` for each multiple `m`) and precomputes each cell's tone `0.7·(ln(rad(n)) / ln(n))^2` (n = 1 is treated as ratio 1); at sampling time every cell uses one compact-support rounded-square kernel (a quartic superellipse through smoothstep, exactly zero before the cell boundary, so the cell lookup never jumps and the field is C1): color is `0.04 + (0.14 + tone − 0.04)·mask + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`, height is `0.8·dome·(0.88 + 0.12·tone) + 0.08·grain`, `occlusion = 1 − 0.4·(1 − mask)`, roughness is fixed at 0.4 and metallic is 0; the cache totals a `Float64Array(2305)` (radicals) of 18,440 B plus a `Float64Array(2304)` (tones) of 18,432 B plus a `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B, 167,944 B in all, all lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Defaults are a 0.3 m nominal tile and 0.0008 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Each sample does a constant number of operations; I did not measure the time, so no performance number is claimed. Measured (tool-run): up to 2304 there are 1400 squarefree numbers, `rad(4) = 2` gives the ratio 1/2, `rad(2048) = 2` gives the smallest ratio 1/11, and `rad(2304) = 6`; on a 256² grid (seeds 0/1/0xffffffff) the lit area (color>0.5) covers 60.65%–60.87%, color is 0.0255–0.0257 to 0.8542–0.8545 with a mean of 0.5278–0.5308, the lowest AO is 0.6 (equal to `1 − 0.4`) and height is at most 0.8472–0.8483 relief; on a 512² grid (seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7) the lit area covers 60.26%–60.57%, color is 0.0251–0.0254 to 0.8547–0.8549 with a mean of 0.5278–0.5290 and height is at most 0.8493–0.8505 relief; for each seed exactly one torus shift (seed 0: (46, 4), 1: (4, 7), 0xffffffff: (17, 42), 7: (30, 23)) makes the colours at the 2304 cell centres match the tones that the test rewrites independently by trial division, within a maximum error of 0.0150 (the error comes from the grain; the test's threshold is 0.03); between seeds 0 and 1, 64.3% of the cell centres differ in colour by more than 0.05, and the light masks (512²) differ on 19.8% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (123.0, 137.3, 101.8), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0296 and the minimum z component is 253. `goldbachtable` adds a Goldbach partition table, bringing the current catalog from 1001 to 1002 kinds (1003 gallery choices including plain). It is a 48×48 grid of squares in which cell (col, row) stands for the even number `n = 2·(row·48 + col + 2)` (4, 6, 8, …, 4610) and is toned by its number of Goldbach partitions `g(n)` (the number of primes `p ≤ n/2` for which `n − p` is also prime): using g(n) directly would brighten steadily with n and show a hard colour step at the table's seam, so I first multiply by `ln(n)²/n` to remove the overall growth, then divide by the largest value in the table and raise it to the power 0.75; what is left is the band structure of the so-called Goldbach comet, where multiples of 6 and 30 are brighter than their neighbours (brightest at n = 2310 = 2·3·5·7·11), in violet on dark purple. The cells are rounded raised squares showing gaps through height and AO, and the seed shifts the whole table around the torus. It shares the cell shape with number-theory tables such as `divisorcount` and `totienttable`, only the values and tones differ. It only shows the partition counts of the first 2304 even numbers; it does not prove or illustrate the Goldbach conjecture.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the toneExponent of 0.75, the toneFloor of 0.14, the toneSpan of 0.7, the violet and dark purple tones and the 0.3 m nominal tile are authored choices. Adjustment record: the first version toned by g(n) divided by its maximum, and the preview showed a dark upper half, a bright lower half and a horizontal band at the table's seam (because g(n) grows with n), so I changed it to multiply by `ln(n)²/n` first; in the second preview the seam shows only a few darker cells (near n = 4) and there is no large colour step overall. I did not keep the test and probe numbers of the first version, and the documentation and tests use only the second version. I did not write claims such as 'numbers just above a power of 2 have few partitions' because I did not verify them. The tests passed on the first run with no need to adjust ranges. The relief reuses 0.0008 without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0280).

At start-up a sieve marks the composite numbers up to `4611`, and for every even `n` the code checks every `q = 2 … n/2` for `q` and `n − q` both being prime to count the partitions (about 2.7 million checks; I measured the sampler build only three times: about 76 ms (first), 17 ms and 16 ms, which is not a benchmark), computes `g(n)·ln(n)²/n`, normalises by the maximum and precomputes each cell's tone `0.7·(ratio/maximum)^0.75`; at sampling time every cell uses one compact-support rounded-square kernel (a quartic superellipse through smoothstep, exactly zero before the cell boundary, so the cell lookup never jumps and the field is C1): color is `0.04 + (0.14 + tone − 0.04)·mask + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`, height is `0.8·dome·(0.88 + 0.12·tone) + 0.08·grain`, `occlusion = 1 − 0.4·(1 − mask)`, roughness is fixed at 0.4 and metallic is 0; the cache totals a `Uint8Array(4611)` of 4,611 B plus two `Float64Array(2304)` (ratio and tone) plus a `Float64Array(128²)`, 172,547 B in all, all lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Defaults are a 0.3 m nominal tile and 0.0008 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Each sample does a constant number of operations; I did not measure its time. `totienttable` adds an Euler totient table, bringing the current catalog from 1000 to 1001 kinds (1002 gallery choices including plain). It is a 48×48 grid of squares in which cell (col, row) stands for the integer `n = row·48 + col + 1` (1 to 2304) and is toned by the totient ratio `φ(n)/n`: the smallest ratio in the table (at n = 210, 48/210) maps to 0 and the ratio 1 (n = 1; primes are only just below 1) to the top, raised to the power 1.5, so primes and numbers with only large prime factors are brightest; even numbers have a ratio of at most 1/2 and multiples of 3 or 5 are pushed down as well, and the table shows distinct vertical stripes (the width 48 is even, so the parity of every column is fixed and the odd columns are brighter), in amber gold on dark brown. The cells are rounded raised squares showing gaps through height and AO, and the seed shifts the whole table around the torus. It shares the cell shape with number-theory tables such as `divisorcount` and `abundantnumbers`, only the values and tones differ. It only shows the function values of the first 2304 positive integers; it does not prove or illustrate any theorem of number theory.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the toneExponent of 1.5, the toneFloor of 0.14, the toneSpan of 0.7, the amber gold and dark brown tones and the 0.3 m nominal tile are authored choices (I looked at only one preview). The cell shape and tone combination reuse the divisorcount parameters and were not retuned for the totient. I did not check whether the vertical stripes are too monotonous: the preview shows clear vertical stripes (because the table width of 48 is even), which is a property of this way of assigning values and not a defect, and I did not break them up by changing the table width. The tests passed on the first run with no need to adjust ranges. The relief reuses 0.0008 without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0296).

At start-up a sieve computes `φ(n)` for `n ≤ 2304` (set `φ(n) = n`, then for every prime `q` and every multiple `m` do `φ(m) −= φ(m)/q`), takes `least = min φ(n)/n`, and precomputes each cell's tone `0.7·((φ(n)/n − least)/(1 − least))^1.5`; at sampling time every cell uses one compact-support rounded-square kernel (a quartic superellipse through smoothstep, exactly zero before the cell boundary, so the cell lookup never jumps and the field is C1): color is `0.04 + (0.14 + tone − 0.04)·mask + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`, height is `0.8·dome·(0.88 + 0.12·tone) + 0.08·grain`, `occlusion = 1 − 0.4·(1 − mask)`, roughness is fixed at 0.4 and metallic is 0; the cache totals an `Int32Array(2305)` of 9,220 B plus a `Float64Array(2304 + 128²)` of 149,504 B, 158,724 B in all, all lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Defaults are a 0.3 m nominal tile and 0.0008 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Each sample does a constant number of operations; I did not measure the time, so no performance number is claimed. Measured (tool-run): n = 210 is the first integer to reach the smallest ratio 48/210, there are 342 primes up to 2304, and the largest ratio among all even numbers is 0.5; on a 256² grid (seeds 0/1/0xffffffff) the lit area (color>0.5) covers 22.23%–23.72%, color is 0.0255–0.0259 to 0.8527–0.8529 with a mean of 0.3109–0.3183, the lowest AO is 0.6 (equal to `1 − 0.4`) and height is at most 0.8459–0.8471 relief; on a 512² grid (seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7) the lit area covers 22.13%–22.78%, color is 0.0252–0.0254 to 0.8536–0.8542 with a mean of 0.3114–0.3142 and height is at most 0.8486–0.8500 relief; for each seed exactly one torus shift (seed 0: (39, 33), 1: (23, 23), 0xffffffff: (19, 33), 7: (42, 4)) makes the colours at the 2304 cell centres match the `φ(n)/n` tones that the test rewrites independently by counting coprime numbers, within a maximum error of 0.0150 (the error comes from the grain; the test's threshold is 0.03); between seeds 0 and 1, 78.5% of the cell centres differ in colour by more than 0.05, and the light masks (512²) differ on 23.6% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (96.6, 80.1, 37.3), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0296 and the minimum z component is 253. I viewed the preview (seed 7): amber rounded squares on dark brown laid out in distinct vertical stripes, the brightest columns being the odd ones. No new API or dependency; Worker, cache and texture ownership follow the existing paths; this paragraph does not claim browser gallery verification.

`spirographtable` adds a spirograph curve table, bringing the current catalog from 999 to 1000 kinds (1001 gallery choices including plain). It is a 6×6 table in which cell (col, row) draws the hypotrochoid made by a wheel of radius `a = col + 1` rolling inside a ring of radius `b = row + 7`, with the pen `0.8·a` from the wheel's centre; a runs from 1 to 6 and b from 7 to 12, so a is always below b; the curve is scaled to lie at most `0.4` cell widths from the cell centre and then rotated as a whole by an angle set by the seed (0 to 0.5 radians), each cell drawing one closed curve, which looks like copper curves with a faint glow on a dark oxblood ground. Where the curve passes over itself a Gaussian sum (not a minimum of distances) is used, so no crease appears. In 13 of the 36 cells a and b have a common factor and the curve closes in fewer than `a` turns; I draw only one closed period and do not retrace. It is only a table of integer ratios of `a` and `b`, not a comparison of pen distances (the pen ratio is fixed at 0.8), and not a real spirograph toy.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the pen ratio of 0.8, the amplitude of 0.4, the line width of 0.016, the glow radius of 0.1 and the copper and dark oxblood tones are authored choices (I looked at two previews: the first used `t ∈ [0, 2π·a)`, which retraces the same curve in cells where a and b have a common factor and doubles its strokes, so I changed it to `t ∈ [0, 2π·a / gcd(a, b))`; the second preview showed no obvious difference to the eye, I made no quantitative comparison and only changed it because it is the mathematically correct closed period). The first preview was only a visual judgement, not a quantitative check. The tests passed after that change; I did not keep the test results from before it, so I make no before-and-after comparison. The relief reuses 0.0008 without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0495).

It uses the same soft union as the rose table (rhodoneatable): each of the 36 cells has a precomputed closed polyline of 360 points (stored in a `Float64Array` in cell widths relative to the cell centre), and at sampling time only the 360 segments of the cell containing the point are walked, computing `Σ exp(−d²/0.016²)` (d is the distance from the point to the segment) and squashing it with `1 − exp(−4·sum)` into the line strength, plus a compact smoothstep glow (radius 0.1; because the curve is at most 0.4 from the cell centre, the glow is exactly zero at the cell boundary and neighbouring cells never jump into each other); color is `0.04 + 0.74·line + 0.12·glow·(1 − line) + 0.02·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`, height is `0.8·line + 0.2·grain`, roughness drops by 0.2 on lines, AO is always 1 and metallic is 0; the cache totals 2×36×360 + 128² = 42,304 Float64 values / 338,432 B, all lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Defaults are a 0.3 m nominal tile and 0.0008 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Every sample walks 360 segments; I measured a single 512² maps generation (seed 7) at about 444 ms, which is one measurement, not a benchmark, and I did not compare it with other materials. Measured (tool-run) at seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7: on a 256² grid the lit area (color>0.5) covers 19.06%–19.20%, color is 0.0303–0.0304 to 0.7892–0.7898 with a mean of 0.2033–0.2035, roughness is 0.2–0.4, AO is always 1 and height is at most 0.9919–0.9984 relief; on a 512² grid the lit area covers 19.07%–19.10%, color is 0.0301–0.0302 to 0.7898–0.7899 with a mean of 0.2034–0.2035 and height is at most 0.9975–0.9992 relief; the maximum color at the four cell corners (0.02 cell widths from the corner) is 0.0487–0.0495; for each of the four seeds, 25–29 of 101 rotation angles (0 to 0.5 radians) put all 36 cells × 96 independently computed curve points on bright pixels (color>0.5), with a best minimum brightness of 0.7702–0.7704 (so the curves really are the hypotrochoids of this table and not a generic bright texture); the light masks (512²) of seeds 0 and 1 differ on 18.5% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (72.6, 43.4, 29.2), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0495, and the AO and alpha checks found nothing wrong. I viewed the preview (seed 7): copper stars, polygons and thin ellipses laid out in a regular grid on dark oxblood, with a faint glow on the edges. No new API or dependency; Worker, cache and texture ownership follow the existing paths; this paragraph does not claim browser gallery verification.

`dodecagridfilled` adds a filled twelve-grid tiling, bringing the current catalog from 998 to 999 kinds (1000 gallery choices including plain). The same twelve-fold patch as `dodecagridtiling` (the same six grids and offsets; 151 tiles, 330 edges, 180 vertices, Euler characteristic 1, vertex valences 2 to 10), but with a tone inside every tile: 30° rhombi are darkest (0.10), 60° rhombi are in the middle (0.18) and squares are brightest (0.26), while the edges are thin pale lime lines, giving lime lines on a dark forest-green ground. The weight of the tone is the same as in `penrosefilled` (a product of one smooth step per edge, C1). The seed only turns the whole patch by a multiple of 30° (12 choices). It is only a small patch, not an infinite tiling, and the tone depends only on the tile shape — it is not a real colouring rule. It shares the tile-filling feature of the multigrid sampler branch with `penrosefilled`, `ammannfilled` and `heptagridfilled`, and only the preset differs.

(2) In the first version I mapped the fill class `k − j − 1` to the rhombus shapes wrongly: I expected classes 0 to 5 to go from wide to narrow and back symmetrically, but the acute angle of a rhombus is set by the angle `(k − j)·360°/7` between the two grid directions, so classes 0 and 5 are 51.4°, classes 1 and 4 are 77.1° and classes 2 and 3 are 25.7°; with `fills` of `[0.10, 0.18, 0.26, 0.26, 0.18, 0.10]` the narrowest 25.7° rhombi were therefore the brightest, the opposite of what I wanted. (3) The crease problem of the tile-filling feature had already been fixed in `penrosefilled`, and the C1 test passed on the first run. The structural checks are the same as for heptagridtiling and are checks of the consistency of the construction, not a formal proof. The relief reuses 0.0007 without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0336).

`penrosefilled` adds a filled Penrose tiling, bringing the current catalog from 995 to 996 kinds (997 gallery choices including plain). The same Penrose rhombus patch as `penrosetiling` (the same pentagrid offsets, 149 rhombi, 323 edges and 175 vertices), but with a tone inside every rhombus: fat rhombi (72°) are brighter and thin rhombi (36°) darker, while the edges remain pale thin lines, giving cream lines and brown-purple rhombi on a dark purple ground. The tone of a rhombus follows the product over its four edges of a weight that tends to 0 (with zero slope) near an edge and is 1 beyond 0.15 edge lengths from every edge, so the tones of neighbouring rhombi never jump and the lines cover the seams. The seed only turns the whole patch by a multiple of 36° (10 choices). It is only a small patch, not an infinite tiling, and the tone depends only on the two rhombus shapes — it is not a real colouring scheme (it obeys no matching rules, for example). It shares the multigrid sampler branch of `penrosetiling` and the other kinds and adds the fields `fills` (the interior tone per grid-pair class), `fillRim` and `fillHeight`; the `fills` of all other materials are 0, so their behaviour is unchanged.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the fat-rhombus tone of 0.2, the thin-rhombus tone of 0.1, the rim width of 0.15, the interior height gain of 0.05, the line tone of 0.7, the cream and dark purple tones and the 0.5 m nominal tile are authored choices (I looked at two previews: the first before, the second after the fix described next). Error record: the first version weighted the interior tone with a smooth step of the minimum of the four edge distances, and the C1 test failed (largest second-difference ratio 51.8) — the minimum has a crease along the bisector of the acute corners where it is still below 0.15, so the tone has a slope discontinuity there; after changing to the product of one smooth step per edge the C1 test passed, and the statistics changed with it (the brightest value dropped from 0.79 to 0.77), so I updated the test's value ranges from the corrected probe output. I wrote the documentation and verification only for the corrected version.

`dodecagridtiling` adds a dodecagrid tiling, bringing the current catalog from 994 to 995 kinds (996 gallery choices including plain). Thin pale violet lines on a dark blue-violet-black ground draw a patch of an aperiodic tiling with approximate twelve-fold rotational symmetry: de Bruijn's multigrid construction with six grids, unit vectors the first six twelfth roots of unity (0°, 30°, …, 150°) and offsets `(0.13, −0.31, 0.22, 0.07, −0.19, 0.08)` (summing to 0), every grid crossing being one rhombus or square — 151 tiles in three kinds by acute angle (41 rhombi of 30°, 70 rhombi of 60° and 40 squares of 90°), 330 unit-length edges and 180 vertices with vertex valences from 2 to 10; the patch is a simply connected disc (Euler characteristic 1); its radius is 6.2 edge lengths and it sits in the middle of a tile with a period of 16 edge lengths, so there is empty space around it and it does not join neighbouring tiles. The seed only turns the whole patch by a multiple of 30° (12 choices). It is only a small patch, not an infinite tiling and not a periodic one; its twelve-fold symmetry is approximate. It shares the multigrid sampler branch of `penrosetiling`, `penrosestar`, `ammannbeenker` and `heptagridtiling` and only the preset differs.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the six offsets are a set I picked by hand (summing to 0, with no scan of other offsets), the patch radius of 6.2, the line radius of 0.09, gain 1.6, the pale violet and dark blue-violet tones and the 0.5 m nominal tile are authored choices (I looked at only one preview). The relief reuses penrosetiling's 0.0007 without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0401). I did not check how this tiling relates to twelve-fold quasicrystal tilings in the literature (for example the Stampfli or Socolar tilings), so I only call it a "dodecagrid tiling" and do not claim it is any of them. `penrosetiling` adds a Penrose tiling, bringing the current catalog from 990 to 991 kinds (992 gallery choices including plain). Thin pale blue lines on a dark navy-black ground draw a patch of the Penrose aperiodic rhombus tiling, built with de Bruijn's pentagrid construction in which every grid crossing is one rhombus: 149 rhombi (95 fat ones of 72°/108° and 54 thin ones of 36°/144°, about 1.76 : 1), 323 unit-length edges and 175 vertices, with vertex valences from 2 to 7; the patch is a simply connected disc (Euler characteristic V − E + F = 1); its radius is 6.2 edge lengths and it sits in the middle of a tile with a period of 16 edge lengths, so there is empty space around it and it does not join neighbouring tiles; the vertices where edges meet are brighter because their weights add up. The seed only turns the whole patch by a multiple of 36° (10 choices). It is only a small patch of the Penrose tiling, not an infinite tiling and not a periodic one; on the torus it is a separate disc.

A dedicated sampler: at build time the patch is generated with the pentagrid construction — the five unit vectors `e_j` are the fifth roots of unity, grid `j` is the set of lines `x·e_j = integer + offsets[j]`, and for every pair `(j, k)` and every integer pair `(r, s)` (−6 to 6) the crossing `x` of the two lines is solved, the other three indices are `ceil(x·e_l − offsets[l])` and the indices of `j` and `k` are `r`, `r+1` and `s`, `s+1`, giving the four corners `Σ K_l e_l` of one rhombus; only rhombi whose centre lies within 6.2 of the origin are kept, shared edges are de-duplicated by a coordinate key (323 of them) and the whole patch is then turned by the seed's rotation; every edge is stored as a midpoint and a half-length vector (four Float64 arrays). Every sample converts its coordinates to tiling units (period 16), takes the point-to-segment distance to every edge, sums the weights `(1 − d²/r²)²` (r = 0.09, value and slope zero at the boundary, C1) and squashes the sum by `1 − exp(−1.6·sum)`; color is `0.06 + 0.78·thread + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`; height is `0.85·thread + 0.15·grain`; roughness drops by 0.1 on lines; AO is always 1; metallic is 0; the cache totals 323×4 + 128² = 17,676 Float64 values / 141,408 B of lattice arithmetic (not total RAM; the crossing and de-duplication tables exist only during construction). Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile and 0.0007 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Every sample walks the 323 edges (skipping those out of reach) and construction walks 1,690 grid crossings; I measured neither, so no performance number is claimed. Measured (tool-run) at seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7: on a 256² grid the lit area (color>0.5) covers 11.54%–11.60%, color is 0.0454–0.0458 to 0.8512–0.8520 with a mean of 0.1450–0.1453, roughness is 0.3–0.4, AO is always 1 and height is at most 0.9811–0.9872 relief; on a 512² grid the lit area covers 11.54%–11.55%, color is 0.0451–0.0452 to 0.8526–0.8538 with a mean of 0.1451–0.1453 and height is at most 0.9887–0.9967 relief; at exactly one rotation step per seed (steps 4, 3, 2 and 1) the colours at every third vertex of the patch match the independently rewritten model of the test (maximum error below 0.03, which is the test's threshold; I did not record the actual maximum per seed); the light masks (512²) of seeds 0 and 1 differ on 12.7% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (31.5, 44.6, 62.7), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0378 and the minimum z component is 253. `kagome` adds kagome, bringing the current catalog from 989 to 990 kinds (991 gallery choices including plain). Thin pale straw lines on a dark olive-green ground draw the kagome lattice: joining the midpoints of the six edges of every honeycomb hexagon in order gives three families of crossing straight lines that form a lattice of alternating hexagons and triangles (the weave of a bamboo basket); 7 columns × 8 rows (56 honeycomb cells, 336 segments in all) with horizontal and vertical periods in the ratio `7√3 : 12` (about 1.04% stretch, so the hexagons and triangles are not regular). The vertices where two segments meet are brighter because their weights add up. The seed only shifts the whole pattern around the torus (in steps of 1/64 of the tile). It is a schematic lattice, not a photograph of a real bamboo basket, and it does not show the over-and-under weaving. It shares the honeycomb-segment sampler branch of `tulle` and `kikko`, and only the preset differs (new `outer` and `innerDegrees` fields).

`kikko` adds kikko, bringing the current catalog from 988 to 989 kinds (990 gallery choices including plain). Thin amber lines on a dark brown ground draw a tortoiseshell hexagonal honeycomb: the outlines of pointy-top hexagons, each with a smaller concentric hexagon of half the radius in its middle; 7 columns × 8 rows (56 hexagons, 504 segments in all: 3 outer edges plus 6 inner edges per hexagon) with horizontal and vertical periods in the ratio `7√3 : 12` (the hexagons are stretched by about 1.04%). It shares the honeycomb-segment sampler branch of `tulle` and only the preset differs (a new `inner` field).

The shared branch gained an `inner` field: `tulle` has `inner` 0 and still 168 segments, so its behaviour is unchanged and the `Tulle as` tests still pass after this change. It reuses the `tulle` honeycomb-segment sampler branch (which now serves `tulle` and `kikko`): at build time, on a pointy-top honeycomb (width `√3`, row spacing 1.5), every hexagon contributes its east, north-east and north-west outer edges and, when `inner > 0`, the 6 edges of a concentric hexagon of radius `inner` (0.5) (each stored as a midpoint and a half-length vector, 504 of them, in four Float64 arrays); every sample converts its coordinates to honeycomb units (horizontal period `7√3`, vertical period 12), takes the point-to-segment distance to the nearest torus image of every segment, sums the weights `(1 − d²/r²)²` (r = 0.1, value and slope zero at the boundary, C1) and squashes the sum by `1 − exp(−1.8·sum)`; color is `0.08 + 0.78·thread + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`; height is `0.85·thread + 0.15·grain`; roughness drops by 0.1 on lines (base 0.35); AO is always 1; metallic is 0; the cache totals 504×4 + 128² = 18,400 Float64 values / 147,200 B of lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Defaults are a 0.3 m nominal tile and 0.0009 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Every sample walks the 504 segments (skipping those out of reach); I did not measure the time, so no performance number is claimed. Measured (tool-run) at seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7: on a 256² grid the lit area (color>0.5) covers 27.66%–27.72%, color is 0.0654–0.0659 to 0.8663–0.8697 with a mean of 0.2772–0.2774, roughness is 0.2505–0.35, AO is always 1 and height is at most 0.9751–0.9895 relief (seeds 0/1/0xffffffff); on a 512² grid the lit area covers 27.27%–27.29%, color is 0.0651–0.0653 to 0.8684–0.8700 with a mean of 0.2773–0.2775 and height is at most 0.9849–0.9917 relief; each seed matches the independently rewritten model of the test (including the inner hexagons) at 48 sample points for exactly 8 of the 64 × 64 candidate torus shifts (maximum error 0.0127–0.0144, roughly the amplitude of the fine grain), and these 8 shifts are the honeycomb's own translation symmetry; the light masks (512²) of seeds 0 and 1 differ on 41.3% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (92.4, 62.8, 23.8), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0414 and the minimum z component is 252. No new API or dependency; Worker, cache and texture ownership follow the existing paths; this paragraph does not claim browser gallery verification.

`vermiculation` adds vermiculation, bringing the current catalog from 987 to 988 kinds (989 gallery choices including plain). A pale tan stone surface carries curving, branching, separate dark worm-like grooves, in the manner of the vermiculated rustication of architectural stone: the pattern comes from periodic Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion in the "worms" regime at `feed 0.078` and `kill 0.061`; the grooves cover about 35% of the area as roughly 20 to 30 separate worms in one connected stone surface; the grooves are darker, rougher (0.85 → about 0.93) and lower, and the stone has a fine grain. The seed changes the initial perturbation of the reaction-diffusion, so every seed lays the worms out differently. It shares the sampler branch of `turingmaze` and only the preset differs (plus a new `baseHeight` field). It is a schematic stone texture, not a photograph or scan of real stone.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; `feed 0.078` and `kill 0.061` come from the commonly quoted Gray-Scott "worms" regime, and I first scanned 12 seeds (0 to 9, 0xffffffff and 12345) with a survey script at 96×96, `seedCells 8`, 6000 and 9000 steps, which gave 35%–37% bright area, 24 to 31 connected components and nearly identical results at 6000 and 9000 steps; the other values (stone colours, groove depth, grain, the 0.4 m nominal tile and relief 0.0015) are authored choices. To make the grooves lower than the stone I added a `baseHeight` field to the shared sampler: `height = baseHeight + ridgeHeight·ridge + grainHeight·grain`, with `baseHeight` set to 0 for `turingmaze`, so its behaviour is unchanged and the `Turing maze as` tests still pass after this change. The maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps is 0.0512 (I did not tune the relief). I only scanned this one parameter pair and did not compare other regimes (for example coral, `feed 0.0545` and `kill 0.062`, which gave a single connected network in the 64×64 scan).

It reuses the `turingmaze` sampler branch (which now serves `turingmaze` and `vermiculation`): at build time `grayScott(96, 8, 0.078, 0.061, 6000, seed)` runs 6000 reaction-diffusion steps on a 96×96 torus grid (only additions, subtractions and multiplications, so it is bit-identical across engines; the result is normalised to [0, 1]) and `latticeField` turns it into a C1 interpolation field; each sample warps its position slightly with 5×5 noise (amplitude 0.05), looks the pattern up and cuts the grooves with `0.5 + 0.5·tanh(9·(pattern − level))` (`level = 0.5 + 0.24·(7×7 noise − 0.5)`) with `ink = ridge·(0.85 + 0.15·7×7 noise)`; color is `0.9 − 0.75·ink + 0.06·(160² fine grain − 0.5)`; height is `0.7 − 0.55·ridge + 0.3·grain`; roughness increases by 0.08 in grooves (base 0.85); AO is always 1; metallic is 0; the cache totals 96² + 5² + 7² + 7² + 160² = 34,939 Float64 values / 279,512 B of lattice arithmetic (not total RAM; the reaction-diffusion scratch arrays exist only during construction). Defaults are a 0.4 m nominal tile and 0.0015 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Measured (tool-run) at seeds 0/1/0xffffffff on a 256² grid: grooves (color<0.5) cover 34.76%–36.02%, stone (color>0.8) covers 58.33%–59.48%, the grooves form 22–28 4-connected regions, the stone is exactly 1 connected region, 4,418–4,610 neighbouring pairs straddle a groove edge, color is 0.1270–0.1331 to 0.9293–0.9297 with a mean of 0.6455–0.6528, roughness is 0.85–0.9297 and height is at most 0.9978–0.9990 relief; the groove masks (256²) of seeds 0 and 1 differ on 46.8% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (161.0, 146.5, 121.9), 36.3% of pixels have r<128, the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0512 and the minimum z component is 252. Single measurements (bun on this machine): building the sampler (including the reaction-diffusion) took about 110–132 ms per seed and the 512² maps about 157 ms — one run for four seeds and one maps run, not a benchmark. I viewed the preview (seed 7): dark curving worm-like grooves on pale tan stone with soft edges. No new API or dependency; Worker, cache and texture ownership follow the existing paths; this paragraph does not claim browser gallery verification.

`minkowskisausage` adds a Minkowski sausage, bringing the current catalog from 986 to 987 kinds (988 gallery choices including plain). A thin pale blue line on a dark navy-black ground traces the order-2 quadratic Koch island (also called the Minkowski sausage): starting from `F+F+F+F` (a square) and replacing every `F` by `F+F−F−FF+F+F−F` twice gives a simple closed loop of 256 unit steps and 256 distinct lattice points (the end returns to the start); its bounding box is about 27×27 cells on a 36×36-cell torus, so there is empty space around it and it does not join neighbouring tiles; the line is a third of a cell wide with a faint glow outside it. The seed only shifts the whole curve around the torus. It is a schematic fractal trace, not a real sausage or a map. It shares the trace sampler branch of `dragoncurve`, `peanocurve` and `levycurve`; only the vertex list differs.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the order 2, the 36×36-cell torus, the one-third-cell line width, the tanh sharpness of 8, the pale blue and dark navy tones and the 0.25 m nominal tile are authored choices. Order 3 would have 2,048 steps and a bounding box of about 107×107 cells, which exceeds the torus sizes this trace branch uses, so I stopped at order 2. The relief reuses dragoncurve's 0.0008 without further tuning (the maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps is 0.0492). I first checked the replacement rule with a small independent script for the number of steps, distinct points and bounding box of order 2, and then chose the torus size.

It reuses the trace sampler branch (which now serves `dragoncurve`, `peanocurve`, `levycurve` and `minkowskisausage`): in Minkowski mode the turtle string `F+F+F+F` has every `F` replaced twice by `F+F-F-FF+F+F-F`, where `F` advances one cell, `+` turns left by 90° and `−` turns right by 90°, giving 257 vertices (the last one back at the start); on a 108×108 lattice the cell points sit at every third coordinate (256 of them) and two connector nodes between consecutive cells fill the gap (512 of them), for 768 lit nodes in total; the curve coordinates get a fixed offset of (7, 7) plus the seed's torus shift; after that it is identical to dragoncurve: `latticeField` blends with the C1 smoothstep and re-sharpens with `0.5 + 0.5·tanh(8·(pattern − 0.5))`, color is `0.06 + 0.76·line + 0.1·glow·(1 − line) + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`, height is `0.8·line + 0.2·grain`, roughness drops by 0.2 on the line (base 0.4) and metallic is 0; the cache totals 108² + 9² + 128² = 28,129 Float64 values / 225,032 B of lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Defaults are a 0.25 m nominal tile and 0.0008 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Measured (tool-run) at seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7 on a 256² grid: the lit area (color>0.5) covers 6.38%–6.43%, color is 0.0458–0.0460 to 0.8331–0.8335 with a mean of 0.1113–0.1114, roughness is 0.2001–0.3999, AO is always 1 and height is at most 0.9887–0.9918 relief; each seed's 108×108 node map equals the curve the test writes independently by block recursion at exactly one torus shift ((28, 24), (31, 33), (30, 32) and (30, 29); 768 lit nodes each); the node maps of seeds 0 and 1 differ on 9.8%; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (26.2, 31.2, 55.1), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0492 and the minimum z component is 252. The test also checks that the independent curve has 257 vertices, ends where it starts and has 256 distinct lattice points (a simple closed loop). `pisanotable` adds a Pisano table, bringing the current catalog from 985 to 986 kinds (987 gallery choices including plain). 48×48 rounded-square tiles; cell (col, row) stands for the integer `n = row × 48 + col + 1` (1 to 2304) and is toned by the Pisano period `π(n)` of the Fibonacci numbers modulo `n` relative to its upper bound `6n`: `0.7·(π(n)/6n)^0.5` — `π(n)` reaches the bound `6n` only for `n = 2·5^k` (10, 50, 250 and 1250 up to 2304, the brightest), and `n` with a short period are dim; the first periods are 1, 3, 8, 6, 20, 24, 16, 12, 24, 60, 10, 24. The whole looks like noise but is a tile mosaic determined by number theory. The seed only moves the whole table around the torus. It is a schematic number-theory pattern, not a real material.

The relief reuses the 0.0008 of the existing table kinds without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0280). In the preview the whole is mid-toned with low contrast and looks like noise. The seed-difference test only asserts that more than 20% of the cells of two seeds' tables differ in tone by more than 0.05, and I did not measure the actual fraction. At build time every `n` steps through the Fibonacci pairs modulo `n` until it returns to (0, 1) (at most `6n` steps); I did not measure this build time, so no performance number is claimed.

`mobiustable` adds a Möbius table, bringing the current catalog from 984 to 985 kinds (986 gallery choices including plain). 48×48 rounded-square tiles; cell (col, row) stands for the integer `n = row × 48 + col + 1` (1 to 2304) and is toned in three classes by the Möbius function `μ(n)`: `μ = 0` when a square divides `n` (dark, 904 of them), `μ = +1` when `n` is a product of an even number of distinct primes (bright violet, 699, including `n = 1`) and `μ = −1` for an odd number (middle grey-violet, 701); because each row has 48 cells, a multiple of 4, the columns holding multiples of 4 are all dark and form dark vertical bars. The seed only moves the whole table around the torus. It is a schematic number-theory pattern, not a real material.

`abundantnumbers` adds an abundant-numbers table, bringing the current catalog from 983 to 984 kinds (985 gallery choices including plain). 48×48 rounded-square tiles; cell (col, row) stands for the integer `n = row × 48 + col + 1` (1 to 2304) and is toned in three classes by comparing `σ(n)` (the sum of all positive divisors of `n`) with `2n`: deficient numbers (`σ(n) < 2n`, 1,732 of them) are dim, abundant numbers (`σ(n) > 2n`, 569 of them) are brighter and perfect numbers (`σ(n) = 2n`: 6, 28 and 496, 3 of them) are the brightest; because each row has 48 cells, a multiple of 12 and of 6, abundant numbers (12, 18, 20, 24, …) line up in conspicuous bright vertical bars while the remaining scattered bright dots are other abundant numbers. The seed only moves the whole table around the torus. It is a schematic number-theory pattern, not a real material.

`xortable` adds an XOR table, bringing the current catalog from 982 to 983 kinds (984 gallery choices including plain). 64×64 rounded-square tiles; the tone of tile (row, col) is proportional to `row XOR col` (bitwise exclusive or) over 63: the main diagonal (`row = col`, result 0) is darkest and the larger `row XOR col` is the brighter the tile, the brightest being yellow-green (lime); the binary digits form nested, Sierpinski-like blocks (the classic "XOR texture", the nim-sum table). The seed only moves the whole table around the torus. It is a schematic mathematical pattern, not a real material.

`paleytable` adds a Paley table, bringing the current catalog from 981 to 982 kinds (983 gallery choices including plain). 61×61 rounded-square tiles; tile (row, col) is the Legendre symbol of `col − row` modulo the prime 61 (the Paley construction): a difference of 0 (the diagonal) takes the middle tone, a nonzero square modulo 61 (a quadratic residue; there are 30 of them) takes bright rose pink and a non-residue takes dark plum; because 61 ≡ 1 (mod 4) the symbol is symmetric, and since the table depends only on `col − row` the whole table shows parallel diagonal bands and repeats seamlessly on the torus. The seed only moves the whole table around the torus, and only `(sx − sy) mod 61` of that shift makes a difference. It is a schematic number-theory pattern, not a real material.

The relief reuses the 0.0008 of the existing table kinds without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0378). I first expected exactly one matching torus shift per seed; the probe showed 61 (the table depends only on `col − row`), so the test now asserts that structure: the `sx − sy` of all 61 shifts is the same, and the `(sx − sy) mod 61` of the four seeds all differ. Measured (tool-run) at seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7: on a 256² grid the lit area (color>0.5) covers 36.34%–36.42%, color is 0.0252–0.0259 to 0.8541–0.8545 with a mean of 0.4012–0.4014, the lowest AO is 0.6 and height is at most 0.8478–0.8486 relief; on a 512² grid the lit area covers 36.35%–36.36%, color is 0.0251–0.0254 to 0.8547–0.8549 with a mean of 0.4011–0.4014, roughness is a constant 0.4, the lowest AO is 0.6 and height is at most 0.8494–0.8504 relief; the colours at the 3,721 tile centres match the table written independently in the test at exactly 61 torus shifts (all with the same `sx − sy`, which is 51, 59, 10 and 23 modulo 61 for the four seeds; maximum error about 0.0148–0.0149, roughly the amplitude of the fine grain); the light masks (512²) of seeds 0 and 1 differ on 37.5% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (116.7, 83.5, 99.1), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0378 and the minimum z component is 253. `hadamardmatrix` adds a Hadamard matrix, bringing the current catalog from 980 to 981 kinds (982 gallery choices including plain). 64×64 rounded-square tiles; tile (row, col) is entry (row, col) of the Sylvester Hadamard matrix: +1 (bright cool white) when the number of 1 bits in the bitwise AND of `row` and `col` is even and −1 (dark blue-grey) when it is odd; row 0 and column 0 are all +1 and every other row has equally many +1 and −1 entries (2,016 of the 4,096 entries are −1), and the whole is built from nested 2×2 blocks. The seed only moves the whole table around the torus. It is a schematic mathematical-matrix pattern, not a real material.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the 64×64 grid, the +1/−1 tones `0.14 + 0.7` / `0.14 + 0.1`, the cool white and dark blue tones and the 0.3 m nominal tile are authored choices. The relief reuses the 0.0008 of the existing table kinds without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0378). The test's 256² grid has only 4 samples per cell and none of them lands on a gap centre, so on 256² the darkest color is 0.0927–0.0936 and the lowest AO 0.7344, unlike the 0.0251–0.0253 and 0.6 of the 512² grid; I first copied the "lowest AO equals 1 − gapOcclusion" assertion from other table kinds, then replaced it with the 256² range and added a sample at the corner shared by four tiles (1/64, 1/64) to confirm the AO is exactly 0.6 there.

`levycurve` adds a Lévy curve, bringing the current catalog from 979 to 980 kinds (981 gallery choices including plain). A thin mint-green line on a dark teal-black ground traces the order-9 Lévy C curve: 512 unit steps in which step `k` heads in direction `i^popcount(k)` (`popcount` is the number of 1 bits in `k`; the directions cycle east, north, west, south), with 416 distinct lattice points and 462 distinct edges — 50 steps retrace an edge already walked, so some segments are drawn twice; its bounding box is about 39×39 cells on a 48×48-cell torus, so there is empty space around it and it does not join neighbouring tiles; the line is a third of a cell wide with a faint glow outside it. The seed only shifts the whole curve around the torus. It is a schematic fractal trace and the curve is not closed. It shares the trace sampler branch of `dragoncurve` and `peanocurve`; only the vertex list differs.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the order 9, the 48×48-cell torus, the one-third-cell line width, the tanh sharpness of 8, the mint and dark teal tones and the 0.25 m nominal tile are authored choices. The relief reuses dragoncurve's 0.0008 without further tuning (the maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps is 0.0543). I first checked the direction rule with a small independent script for the vertex and edge counts (order 9: 416 distinct points, 462 distinct edges, bounding box x −7 to 31, y −15 to 23) and then chose the torus size and offsets.
